1.title: Tool Distribution, toolchoice, MCP Servers and Built-in Tools
1.text: Welcome to Module six: Tool Distribution, tool choice, M C P Servers and Built-in Tools. This module covers task statements two point three to two point five: tool distribution, tool choice, m c p servers and built-in tools. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. Why too many tools hurt, and how to scope tools to roles. The three tool choice modes: auto, any, and forced selection. M C P (Model Context Protocol) server scoping: project dot M C P dot Jason versus user home dot Claude dot json, environment variable expansion, resources. Choosing among Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob.

1.title: Case Check-In: Birchwood Supply's Synthesis Agent Wanders
1.text: Our running case is Birchwood Supply. Birchwood Supply's Synthesis Agent Wanders. The research system gave every subagent all eighteen tools. The synthesis agent started running web searches itself, and tool choices became unreliable. Meanwhile about four in five of its "verification" needs are simple fact checks (a date, a name).

1.title: Distributing Tools Across Agents
1.text: Distributing Tools Across Agents. Too many tools (eighteen instead of four or five) increases decision complexity and degrades selection reliability. Agents given tools outside their specialization misuse them (a synthesis agent trying web searches). Scoped tool access (least privilege): each agent gets only the tools its role needs, plus a few narrow cross-role tools for frequent needs. Replace generic tools with constrained ones: fetch url to load document, which validates that the U R L (uniform resource locator) is a document U R L.

1.title: Distributing Tools Across Agents, continued
1.text: Distributing Tools Across Agents, continued. Scoped cross-role tool: give the synthesis agent a small verify fact tool for the common simple checks, and route complex verification through the coordinator to the web search agent.

1.title: Distributing Tools Across Agents, continued
1.text: Distributing Tools Across Agents, continued. The figure shows this: Scoped tool sets: each agent gets the few tools its role needs; a narrow verify fact tool serves the frequent simple check, and complex cases still go through the coordinator. Exam tip: "Reduce round-trips but keep reliability" to a scoped tool for the common case (least privilege), with the coordinator still handling the rare complex case. Giving all web-search tools to the synthesis agent over-provisions it.

1.title: toolchoice
1.text: tool choice. "auto" (default with tools). Behavior: The model may call a tool or answer in text. Use it when: Normal agent behavior. "any". Behavior: The model must call a tool, but picks which. Use it when: You need structured output and several schemas fit; the document type is unknown. Forced: {"type": "tool", "name": "..."}. Behavior: The model must call that named tool. Use it when: A specific step must run first, for example extract metadata before enrichment tools; then handle later steps in follow-up turns.

1.title: toolchoice, continued
1.text: tool choice, continued. The figure shows this: tool choice: auto may answer in text, any must call some tool, and a forced selection must call the named tool. In current A P I (application programming interface) documentation, forced tool use (any and tool) returns an error on some models: it is not supported with manual extended thinking, and it returns a four hundred error on Claude Opus five point five, Sonnet five point five, Fable five point one and Mythos five point one. The documented alternatives are auto with strict tool use (schema-valid inputs) or structured outputs (output config.format). The exam guide still teaches "any" and forced selection, so answer as the guide teaches; in real code, check the model's support first. As of eight November two thousand twenty-six.

1.title: MCP Servers in Claude Code and Agent Workflows
1.text: M C P Servers in Claude Code and Agent Workflows. The figure shows this: Two homes for M C P servers: project dot M C P dot Jason for shared team tooling and user home dot Claude dot json for personal or experimental servers; the agent gets the tools of all of them.

1.title: MCP Servers in Claude Code and Agent Workflows, continued
1.text: M C P Servers in Claude Code and Agent Workflows, continued. Where do shared team servers go? Project scope: dot M C P dot Jason in the repository, shared through version control. Where do personal or experimental servers go? User scope: home dot Claude dot json, not shared. How to keep tokens out of the repo? Environment variable expansion in dot M C P dot Jason, for example the github token variable. Are all servers' tools available together? Yes: tools from all configured servers are discovered at connection time and available simultaneously. How to reduce exploratory calls? Expose content catalogs as M C P resources (issue summaries, documentation hierarchy, database schemas).

1.title: MCP Servers in Claude Code and Agent Workflows, continued
1.text: M C P Servers in Claude Code and Agent Workflows, continued. Build or reuse? Use an existing community server for standard integrations (for example Jira); build a custom server only for team-specific workflows. Agent prefers built-in Grep over a better M C P tool? Enhance the M C P tool's description to explain capabilities and outputs in detail.

1.title: MCP Servers in Claude Code and Agent Workflows, continued
1.text: M C P Servers in Claude Code and Agent Workflows, continued. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: MCP Servers in Claude Code and Agent Workflows, continued
1.text: M C P Servers in Claude Code and Agent Workflows, continued. Current Claude Code documentation names three scopes: local (default, stored in home dot Claude dot json, private to you in one project), project (dot M C P dot Jason, shared) and user (all your projects). When a name appears in several, local beats project beats user. Project servers need your approval in interactive use. Expansion supports dollar brace V A R and dollar brace V A R colon dash default. M C P tools appear as M C P, then the server name, then the tool name, and newer versions can defer loading M C P tool definitions until needed. As of eight November two thousand twenty-six. Exam tip: Shared team servers go in the project dot M C P dot Jason with an environment variable reference tokens; personal or experimental servers go in the user home dot Claude dot json.

1.title: Built-in Tools
1.text: Built-in Tools. Grep. Use it to...: Search file contents (function names, error messages, imports). Remember: First step to find entry points and callers. Glob. Use it to...: Find files by name pattern (any test T S X file). Remember: Path patterns, not contents. Read. Use it to...: Load a whole file. Remember: To follow imports and trace flow. Write. Use it to...: Create or fully rewrite a file. Remember: Replaces the content. Edit. Use it to...: Targeted change by matching unique text. Remember: Fails if the text is not unique. Bash. Use it to...: Run shell commands (tests, git). Remember: Use for execution, not for searching code.

1.title: Built-in Tools, continued
1.text: Built-in Tools, continued. The figure shows this: Choosing a built-in tool: Grep for content, Glob for names, Read for whole files, Edit for unique targeted changes, and Read plus Write when Edit has no unique anchor. When Edit fails because the anchor text appears more than once: Read the file, then Write the corrected full file (the reliable fallback). Build understanding incrementally: Grep for entry points, Read to follow imports and trace flows, rather than reading every file up front.

1.title: Built-in Tools, continued
1.text: Built-in Tools, continued. Trace usage through wrapper modules: first list the exported names, then Grep each name across the codebase. Exam tip: Edit needs unique anchor text; when it is not unique, Read then Write. Search content with Grep and find names with Glob.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Tool count: four to five relevant tools beat eighteen; too many degrade selection. Scoping: Role-specific tools; narrow cross-role tool (verify fact); constrained replacement (load document for fetch url). tool choice: auto (text or tool), any (must call some tool), forced {"type":"tool","name":...} (must call that tool). M C P scopes: Project dot M C P dot Jason (shared), user home dot Claude dot json (personal), an environment variable reference expansion. M C P behavior: All servers' tools available at once; resources expose catalogs; prefer community servers; enrich tool descriptions. Grep or Glob: Grep equals contents; Glob equals file names or paths. Read or Write or Edit: Read whole, Write replaces, Edit needs unique text; Edit fails to Read plus Write. Exploration: Grep entry points to Read to follow imports; for wrappers list exports then grep each name.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Birchwood's synthesis agent has all eighteen tools, keeps performing its own web searches, and picks wrong tools. What is the best change? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Fewer, role-specific tools improve selection and prevent cross-specialization misuse.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. About four in five of the synthesis agent's verification needs are quick lookups (a date, a name, a figure); the rest need real research. Each round trip through the coordinator adds delay. Which approach is best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. A narrow tool covers the common case; the rest keeps the existing coordination. Full tool access over-provisions the agent, batching creates blocking dependencies and speculative caching cannot predict needs.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. A pipeline must always run extract metadata before any enrichment tool. Which setting makes the model call that tool first? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Forced selection guarantees the named tool is called; subsequent steps continue in later turns.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. A document extraction service receives invoices, receipts or contracts and has one extraction schema per type. The type is unknown up front, and the model sometimes replies in plain text. Which tool choice is best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. "any" guarantees a tool call while letting the model pick the matching schema.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Where should a team-shared Jira M C P server be configured, with its token kept out of version control? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Project scope shares the server through version control; environment variable expansion keeps secrets out of the file.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. A developer wants to try a new experimental M C P server without affecting teammates. Where should it go? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Personal and experimental servers belong in user scope; project scope would add it for everyone.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. A custom M C P search tool is far more capable than Grep, but the agent keeps using built-in Grep. What helps most? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Better descriptions guide selection toward the more capable tool.

2.title: Practice Question 8
2.text: Question eight. Agents repeatedly make exploratory calls to learn which documentation pages exist. Which M C P feature reduces this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Resources expose content catalogs so the agent can see what is available without exploratory calls.

2.title: Practice Question 9
2.text: Question nine. An Edit call fails because the target text appears in six places. What is the most reliable approach? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. When there is no unique anchor, Read plus Write is the dependable fallback.

2.title: Practice Question 10
2.text: Question ten. An engineer must find every caller of calculate Total in an unfamiliar repository. Which first step is best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Grep finds entry points by content; Read then follows imports. Reading everything up front wastes context.

2.title: Practice Question 11
2.text: Question eleven. Select two. Which two statements about M C P configuration in Claude Code are correct? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and D. The project file is shared and can reference an environment variable reference values, so secrets stay out of version control. User scope is personal, and tools from all configured servers are available together.

2.title: Practice Question 12
2.text: Question twelve. Select two. Which two statements about tool choice are correct? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and B. any guarantees a tool call but lets the model choose, and a forced selection names the tool. auto allows either a tool call or text.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all twelve answers. Question one: D. Question two: B. Question three: C. Question four: C. Question five: A. Question six: B. Question seven: B. Question eight: B. Question nine: B. Question ten: C. Question eleven: B and D. Question twelve: A and B. In the next module, we continue the course.
